newsitem.title: POLAND: French firms urged to boost Polish investment.
newsitem.headline: French firms urged to boost Polish investment.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac on Thursday urged French firms to boost their investment in Poland, reflecting a concern that they are under-represented.
"I would like to ask all representatives of French firms... to show a more conquering spirit," Chirac, on an official visit until Friday, told a meeting of French and Polish executives.
He earlier told parliament: "The image of France, in Poland, and this part of Europe, is still that of a timid entrepreneur... We must and can do better."

Polish Privatisation Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek said France had fallen behind countries such as Germany or Italy because, until 1995, its firms were cautious about Poland, which shed communism in 1989 and then had to overcome economic chaos.
"Only in 1995 did French investors begin to trust Poland and started to come here," Kaczmarek told Reuters.

France is only the sixth biggest investor, trailing the United States, Germany, international corporations, Italy and Holland, according to a July report of the government's Foreign Investment Agency (PAIZ).
France is also only Poland's fifth biggest trading partner, with economic exchange of $2.2 billion in 1995 and a Polish deficit of $600 million.
In the last five years, French investors brought a total of $657 million, compared to $2.4 billion contributed by the United States and $1.3 billion by Germany.

With one exception, all significant French investment projects came after 1994, when the Polish economy was well advanced on a growth track, which reached seven percent last year and is forecast at around six percent in 1996.
France's biggest single investor is Thomson Consumer Electronics, which arrived in the early 1990s and brought $185 million to make televisions in Piaseczno near Warsaw.

Investors began flooding in last year, when tyre maker Michelin bought the north Poland Stomil factory for $112 million. Lafarge began buying stakes in Polish cement plants and tobacco firm Seita contributed $64 million to acquire the state-owned Radom cigarette factory.
French retail networks Auchan and Leclerc launched plans to open dozens of supermarkets within the next few years.
"The French are trying to catch up," Kaczmarek said.
But several snags in the two countries' economic relations have deterred French investment.

In the most serious, France Telecom has launched international arbitration proceedings against the Polish government over its refusal to grant a joint venture, involving the French company, a licence to expand operations.
The privatisation ministry is also delaying a decision on selling Poland's large news-stand network Ruch SA to a consortium involving French news distributor Hachette.
Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said he discussed with Chirac ways to eliminate the problems and sources close to both leaders said that Chirac lobbied for his country's firms.
Before the visit, Kwasniewski told reporters it was politically important for Poland to lure more French capital and trade to balance out its foreign economic relations.
Germany currently accounts for 38 percent of Polish trade.
A source close to Chirac's office, who asked not to be named, said he urged Poland to buy European military equipment when modernising its forces to meet NATO standards.
Poland aims to buy 100 fighter aircraft and French Dassault's Mirage 2000 is competing for the deal, among others, with Lockheed Martin's F-16 and McDonnell Douglas' F-18 from the United States.
